documents.unit: Office of the Provost / AI Working Group
documents.title: Michigan Tech Syllabus Guidance
documents.summary: The Provost's AI Working Group offers three adaptable syllabus templates (general permission, conditional permission, prohibition) plus a sample HU 3015 writing policy. Instructors choose and adapt a template; all templates call for transparency, student responsibility and provisional policy.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no single rule but offers templates 'categorized into three tiers—General Permission, Conditional Permission, and Prohibition' that 'are adaptable based on individual course requirements', so the decision is handed to instructors and the tiers are listed.

units.why: The page frames the three templates as a tiered system; 'categorized into three tiers' is a named-tier structure, so P05 fits better than P04 (who decides, without naming levels).
units.anchor: categorized into three tiers—General Permission, Conditional Permission, and Prohibition
units.frag_start: These templates, categorized into
units.policy: The syllabus templates are categorized into three tiers: General Permission, Conditional Permission, and Prohibition, adaptable to individual course requirements.

units.why: The templates guide instructors in setting their own course GAI policies, so the rule is set per course by the instructor ('adaptable based on individual course requirements').

units.frag_start: The AI Working Group at
units.policy: Instructors establish generative AI use policies within their own courses using adaptable templates.

units.why: The work group 'encourages' pairing the templates with AI-literacy class discussion; a recommendation to teach AI literacy as a skill, so P44 rather than a stance type.

units.policy: Instructors are advised to regularly consult the Academic Integrity Policy, Research Integrity Policies and the Provost's AI Resources page to stay informed about the latest AI tools and policy updates.

documents.title: 1.20 Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools
documents.summary: University Policy 1.20 sets five high-level considerations for any affiliate using generative AI in a university capacity: data submission, consent, output review, compliance and disclosure. It is not classroom-specific and lets units devise their own consistent policies.
documents.stance_why: The policy states AI 'can be used to significant positive benefit' and gives five considerations (avoid tier 1 data, consent, review, compliance, disclose) rather than banning or delegating, so AI use is allowed with conditions: permit.

units.why: The introduction says AI 'can be used to significant positive benefit but can also be misused', a balanced framing statement of purpose, P56.
units.anchor: can be used to significant positive benefit but can also be misused with significant negative
units.frag_start: Like other technological developments, generative
units.policy: Generative AI can be used to significant positive benefit but can also be misused with significant negative consequences.

units.why: The purpose and scope sentence names the interests protected and who is covered, an institution-level framework, P56.
units.anchor: this policy provides high level considerations and guidance for University affiliates
units.frag_start: To ensure responsible use of tools
units.policy: To ensure responsible use of evolving tools and protect the reputation, intellectual property, equity and privacy of MTU and its affiliates, the policy provides high level considerations and guidance for University affiliates using AI tools in their university-affiliated capacity.

units.why: 'Administrative units of MTU may devise their own AI-related policies' delegates to units; this is unit-level rule setting (P04), the closest fit.
units.anchor: Administrative units of MTU may devise their own AI-related policies and procedures
units.frag_start: Administrative units of MTU may
units.policy: Administrative units of MTU may devise their own AI-related policies and procedures consistent with this policy and other applicable university policies, protocols, and procedures.

units.why: Consideration I says 'Avoid submitting MTU data classified as tier 1' to AI tools, a data-protection rule, P50.
units.anchor: Avoid submitting MTU data classified as tier 1 (confidential or restricted)
units.frag_start: Avoid submitting MTU data classified
units.policy: Avoid submitting MTU data classified as tier 1 (confidential or restricted) with AI tools.

units.why: The context says 'there is no expectation of privacy when using AI tools' and only public or non-sensitive data should be shared; P50.
units.anchor: only publicly available or non-sensitive data should be shared with AI tools
units.frag_start: Generally, there is no expectation
units.policy: Generally, there is no expectation of privacy when using AI tools, as input data may be used for training or shared as output; only publicly available or non-sensitive data should be shared with AI tools.

units.why: Tier 1 data may be used only with written consent of the CIO, CISO or General Counsel where a contract protects MTU data: an exception procedure for data, P50.
units.anchor: only with the written consent of the
units.frag_start: Where a contract or other legal
units.policy: Where a contract or other legal agreement provides explicit protections to MTU data, tier 1 data may be used with an AI tool only with the written consent of the Chief Information Officer, Chief Information Security Officer, or General Counsel.

units.why: Consideration II: 'Obtain the consent of data owners before sharing any data with AI tools', a data-privacy rule, P50.
units.anchor: Obtain the consent of data owners before sharing any data with AI tools
units.frag_start: Obtain the consent of data owners
units.policy: Obtain the consent of data owners before sharing any data with AI tools.

units.why: 'Inform participants if AI tools will be used in meetings' and allow opt-out is disclosure of AI use to those affected; P47 is closest.
units.anchor: Inform participants if AI tools will be used in meetings or other shared engagements
units.frag_start: Inform participants if AI tools
units.policy: Inform participants if AI tools will be used in meetings or other shared engagements; participants must have the ability to opt-out of such use.

units.why: If the data owner cannot be identified 'the data cannot be used with any AI tools', an explicit prohibition tied to data ownership, P50.
units.anchor: If the data owner cannot be identified, the data cannot be used with any AI
units.frag_start: If the data owner cannot
units.policy: If the data owner cannot be identified, the data cannot be used with any AI tools.

units.why: 'Even publicly available data may be protected by copyright' raises IP limits on inputs: P52.
units.anchor: even publicly available data may be protected by copyright and/or may have limitations on use
units.frag_start: Note that even publicly available data
units.policy: Even publicly available data may be protected by copyright and/or may have limitations on use.

units.why: Consideration III: 'Review the output of AI tools prior to use or publication to ensure accuracy and relevance', P31.
units.anchor: Review the output of AI tools prior to use or publication to ensure accuracy and
units.frag_start: Review the output of AI tools
units.policy: Review the output of AI tools prior to use or publication to ensure accuracy and relevance.

units.why: The context names bias in training data as a risk, P53 (the concern) rather than P31 (the instruction).
units.anchor: AI tools may exhibit bias based on the data used for training
units.frag_start: Research has shown that AI tools
units.policy: AI tools may exhibit bias based on the data used for training and such bias may be incorporated into their output.

units.why: 'MTU affiliates must evaluate the output of any AI tool to ensure that it is accurate, relevant' is a must-verify rule, P31.
units.anchor: MTU affiliates must evaluate the output of any AI tool to ensure that it is
units.frag_start: MTU affiliates must evaluate the output
units.policy: MTU affiliates must evaluate the output of any AI tool to ensure that it is accurate, relevant, and does not infringe on copyright or violate any laws or ethical norms based on its intended use.

units.why: Consideration IV: 'Ensure compliance with applicable laws, university policies, and relevant terms of use or license agreements', P52 (terms of use and licenses).
units.anchor: Ensure compliance with applicable laws, university policies, and relevant terms of use or license agreements
units.frag_start: Ensure compliance with applicable laws
units.policy: Ensure compliance with applicable laws, university policies, and relevant terms of use or license agreements provided by AI tools or the data being supplied to the tools.

units.why: The policy admits it 'cannot address all potential use cases', so users must identify relevant laws and terms themselves; P52 for contract and license terms.
units.anchor: identify and understand all relevant laws, policies, contract terms, and other such requirements
units.frag_start: it is critical that anyone intending
units.policy: Anyone intending to utilize AI tools must identify and understand all relevant laws, policies, contract terms and other requirements before leveraging AI tools and before utilizing any output.

units.why: Consideration V requires disclosure where the receiving entity demands it and in all cases when AI use exceeds 25% of the final product, P24 with a concrete threshold.
units.anchor: Disclose use of AI tools as required by the entity receiving the AI-facilitated content
units.frag_start: Disclose use of AI tools as required
units.policy: Disclose use of AI tools as required by the entity receiving the AI-facilitated content, and in all cases where such use represents a significant component of the final product or deliverable (more than 25%).

units.why: The context grounds disclosure in 'academic integrity and professional ethics' requiring 'honesty and transparency'; a principle statement, P56.
units.anchor: Academic integrity and professional ethics require honesty and transparency
units.frag_start: Academic integrity and professional ethics
units.policy: Academic integrity and professional ethics require honesty and transparency in their respective environments, which extends to work developed by students, employees and other affiliates for or on behalf of MTU.

units.why: 'Failure to disclose... could lead to allegations of plagiarism or academic or professional misconduct' makes nondisclosure the violation, P28.
units.anchor: Failure to disclose the use of AI tools in the development of any deliverable could
units.frag_start: Failure to disclose the use of AI tools
units.policy: Failure to disclose the use of AI tools in the development of any deliverable could lead to allegations of plagiarism or academic or professional misconduct, adverse impact on reputation and limitations on grants, contracts and committee participation.

units.why: 'Encouraged to disclose any use... required if the use represents a significant component' restates the two-level disclosure rule, P24.
units.anchor: MTU affiliates are encouraged to disclose any use of AI tools, and are required to
units.frag_start: MTU affiliates are encouraged to disclose
units.policy: MTU affiliates are encouraged to disclose any use of AI tools, and are required to do so if the use represents a significant component of the final product or deliverable.

units.why: The definition of generative AI sets the policy's scope, P61.
units.anchor: artificial intelligence tools that have been trained with datasets and which can create new and
units.frag_start: Generative artificial intelligence: For purposes
units.frag_end: prompted by the user of the tool.
units.policy: Generative artificial intelligence refers to AI tools trained with datasets that can create new and original content (audio, video, pictures, text, etc.) when prompted by the user.

units.why: The definition of Affiliate sets who the policy covers, P61.
units.anchor: Affiliate: any individual or group officially attached to the university
units.frag_start: Affiliate: any individual or group
units.policy: An affiliate is any individual or group officially attached to the university, such as a contractor, an organization with which the university has another applicable agreement, or a consultant.

documents.unit: Office of the Provost / AI Working Group
documents.title: AI FAQs for Faculty and Staff
documents.summary: The Provost's FAQ for faculty and staff says Michigan Tech lets instructors and programs decide how GAI is used in classes, and urges clear syllabus statements. It also advises faculty to learn AI tools, discuss approaches within units, and be cautious about detection software, and gives research-use guidance.
documents.stance_why: The FAQ states 'Michigan Tech currently allows for instructors and programs to decide how GAI can and may be used in classroom settings', so it sets no stance itself and delegates.

units.why: The answer to the research question tells faculty to document where and how GAI tools are used, tied to funder and publisher policies, P62.
units.anchor: Document where and how GAI tools are used.
units.frag_start: Document where and how GAI
units.policy: Faculty using GAI tools in research should document where and how GAI tools are used, because documentation may be needed to align with funding agency and publisher policies.

units.why: Faculty 'should also be aware of any guidance' from funders and publishers: deferring to venue or funder rules, P62.
units.anchor: Faculty should also be aware of any guidance for the use of such tools
units.frag_start: Faculty should also be aware
units.policy: Faculty should be aware of any guidance for the use of such tools in proposal development and on projects from their funding agency and publishers.

units.why: 'Researchers must understand the bias... in particular when working with human subjects data' is about limits and bias of AI in research, P53.
units.anchor: Researchers must understand the bias that may exist or be produced by such tools
units.frag_start: Understand the limitations of such systems.
units.policy: Researchers need to ensure that systems report accurate and repeatable results and must understand the bias that may exist or be produced by such tools, in particular when working with human subjects data.

units.why: Faculty should protect data under laws such as FERPA, HIPAA and export controls, P50.
units.anchor: Protect their data under any applicable data privacy laws
units.frag_start: Protect their data under any
units.policy: Faculty using GAI tools should protect their data under any applicable data privacy laws, e.g., FERPA, HIPAA, Export Controls.

units.why: 'Michigan Tech currently allows for instructors and programs to decide' is the explicit delegation of the classroom rule, P04.
units.anchor: allows for instructors and programs to decide how GAI can and may be used in
units.frag_start: Michigan Tech currently allows for instructors
units.policy: Michigan Tech currently allows instructors and programs to decide how GAI can and may be used in classroom settings.

units.why: Instructors 'should make sure to clarify to students on what is acceptable and unacceptable use... in their syllabus and assignments' requires the AI statement in syllabus and assignments, P09.
units.anchor: instructors should make sure to clarify to students on what is acceptable and unacceptable use
units.frag_start: With this flexibility, instructors should
units.policy: Instructors should make sure to clarify to students what is acceptable and unacceptable use of GAI tools and systems in their syllabus and assignments.

units.why: 'The key issue is being clear and transparent with students about your stance on AI' repeats the communication expectation; coded P09.
units.anchor: The key issue is being clear and transparent with students about your stance on AI
units.frag_start: The key issue is being clear
units.policy: The key issue is being clear and transparent with students about your stance on AI for use in the course.

units.why: Instructors 'need to be prepared to' understand AI tools and become familiar with what students might use; faculty learning AI before setting policy, P63.
units.anchor: it's important to become familiar with AI tools that might be employed by students
units.frag_start: Students are largely ahead of faculty
units.policy: Faculty should not opt out of understanding AI; it is important to become familiar with AI tools that might be employed by students to complete work in the course.

units.why: Faculty 'can and should identify uses of AI compatible with their course goals and ... integrate it into their courses to prepare students for AI use in their future area of work': career preparation, P44.
units.anchor: integrate it into their courses to prepare students for AI use in their future area
units.frag_start: faculty can and should identify uses
units.policy: Faculty can and should identify uses of AI compatible with their course goals and identify ways to integrate it into their courses to prepare students for AI use in their future area of work.

units.why: Advice to give GAI the assignment prompt and see what it generates prompts instructors to test assignments against AI, which feeds assignment redesign, P35 (not P63 since the aim is assignment design).
units.anchor: provide GAI with your task/assignment prompt and see what kind of material it generates
units.frag_start: a first step might be to provide GAI
units.policy: A first step for instructors might be to provide GAI with their task/assignment prompt and see what material it generates, but they must be prepared to do more than just copy and paste their assignments.

units.why: 'Instructors must recognize that there is not a single right way to approach AI' reinforces discipline-level discretion, P04.
units.anchor: there is not a single right way to approach AI in their courses, programs, or
units.frag_start: Instructors must recognize that there
units.policy: Instructors must recognize that there is not a single right way to approach AI in their courses, programs, or scholarship; approaches will differ by discipline.

units.why: 'Learn more about what principles of transparency, accountability, and ethical use look like in your field' advises instructors to learn principles of AI use in their field, P63.
units.anchor: Learn more about what principles of transparency, accountability, and ethical use look like in your
units.frag_start: Learn more about what principles
units.policy: Instructors should learn what principles of transparency, accountability, and ethical use look like in their field of study.

units.why: 'Build in opportunities for faculty in your academic unit to share their approach' especially for sequential courses; faculty communities, P63.
units.anchor: Build in opportunities for faculty in your academic unit to share their approach to classroom
units.frag_start: Build in opportunities for faculty
units.policy: Faculty should build in opportunities within their academic unit to share their approach to classroom use of AI (policy statement, pedagogical uses, guidance to students), particularly for courses that are sequential or prerequisites.

units.why: The FAQ worries AI use may 'interfere with the development of key skills and knowledge necessary for success in the program', a rationale about protecting skill-building, P41.
units.anchor: interfere with the development of key skills and knowledge necessary for success in the program
units.frag_start: It is important to understand the student experience
units.policy: It is important to understand the student experience of navigating the curriculum and whether AI tool usage might be disruptive or confusing, or interfere with the development of key skills and knowledge necessary for success in the program.

units.why: Faculty are told to commit to exploring pedagogical resources and developing their own AI skills, P63.
units.anchor: Commit to exploring these resources and developing your own skills in these areas.
units.frag_start: Commit to exploring these resources
units.policy: Faculty should commit to exploring pedagogical resources and developing their own skills in AI.

units.why: Faculty are told to think through detection programs, noting many universities have opted not to employ detection products; guidance toward not relying on detectors, P39.
units.anchor: Many universities have opted not to employ commercial products that promise detection
units.frag_start: Many universities have opted not
units.policy: Faculty should think through the implications of detection programs; many universities have opted not to employ commercial AI-detection products.

units.why: 'Detection software is not yet accurate enough to warrant the number of false positives' states detectors are unreliable, P39.
units.anchor: Detection software is not yet accurate enough to warrant the number of false positives
units.frag_start: Detection software is not yet accurate
units.policy: Detection software is not yet accurate enough to warrant the number of false positives, and it erodes the relationship of trust and focus on good-faith learning between students and teachers.

documents.title: About Michigan Tech's Academic Integrity Policy
documents.summary: The Dean of Students' academic integrity page defines misconduct and, under cheating, adds one sentence making GAI use that the instructor prohibits or that does not follow University Policy 1.20 an integrity violation. The rest of the page concerns misconduct generally.
documents.stance_why: The only AI statement is that GAI use 'in ways that are prohibited by the instructor or that do not comport with University Policy 1.20' is a violation, which makes the instructor the one who sets the rule, so the document delegates.

units.why: The sentence classes prohibited or non-compliant GAI use as an integrity violation, P36; it also makes the instructor's prohibition the standard (P04), but the misconduct classification is the main content.
